title: Don’t Count Out the Country House
author: Will Tanner
text:
Paul Clarkson/Wentworth Woodhouse in the snow

The wealthy of Britain, and those of the Western world more broadly, are today expected to surrender rather than pass on the fortune they have spent their lives creating. The “haves” are tolerated, and at times even encouraged, to spend exorbitantly on pleasure and frivolity, so long as upon death they hand whatever remains over to bureaucrats putatively aiding the have-nots. This is sometimes made explicit and termed Die with Zero by some, “The Giving Pledge” by others. What is less known, or if known, rarely discussed, is that this attitude is the exact antithesis of what made Western civilization great in the first place. In almost every era other than our own, the role of wealth was understood to be for building an enduring dynasty to carry on the values and legacy of those who had contributed so much to society.
Before the Great War, British society expected that those born into wealth, whether as a result of a dynast landing at Pevensey Bay with William the Conqueror or an uncle industrializing Manchester, would spend their privileged lives in roles of leadership and public service, before passing on their carefully stewarded riches for their heirs to do the same. When the British philosopher and politician Edmund Burke described society as “a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born,” he was merely making explicit the way of life practiced by his contemporaries and their ancestors. This sense of solidarity with both the past and future was felt by them as well, and was the basis of the British aristocracy’s continuity in rule for almost a thousand years. 
In 1914, Britain marched to war led by those who, like war-hero Hugh Grosvenor, traced their blood all the way back to the age of chivalry. That a landed feudal elite could lead a modern industrial state was a testament to its deep ties to the communities from which it drew its power. Over the centuries, it led and developed Britain with a sensibility distinctly lacking in our age of bureaucratic rule. As modern bureaucracy hits seemingly intractable problems of governance and entropy—essentially choking out prospects for a worthwhile future—perhaps this successful ethos and the unique conditions under which it arose are worth a close study by those who wish to build a better tomorrow. 
The Birth of Aristocracy
When the English gentry first solidified in the Late Middle Ages, its role was military leadership, which it exercised with a mailed gauntlet, not a gentleman’s glove. The then-Earls of Northumberland and their gentry retainers, families like the Plumptons, ruled over domains both vast and modest while battling in the courts and, if needed, on the fields in order to expand their holdings. As English historian Adam Nicolson writes in his book The Gentry, this “unforgiving assertion of violent authority” separated the medieval gentry from the landed elite of later periods.
This early gentry also served in local leadership positions—acting as justices of the peace, high sheriffs, or knights of the shire—that have long defined their place in country society. Above the ordinary landed gentry was the titled nobility—dukes, earls, and barons—the most powerful tier of Britain’s landowning class. They increased from a mere five dozen or so in the Tudor period to around five hundred by the 19th century, with most of the new titles coming from old landed families purchasing or earning titles as they increased in wealth and prestige following the dissolution of the monasteries. The titled nobility, also known as the peers, or Lords, tended to invest their political energy in national and imperial politics while the gentry governed the counties. However, all of the landed elite were by necessity intimately involved in both local and national affairs. 
In 1215, the great barons and their gentry retainers forced King John to accede to the Magna Carta, balancing the rights of the landed aristocracy against the centralized power of the monarchy. When those rights were threatened, the aristocracy waged barons’ wars to defend them. In 1265, nobleman Simon de Montfort led the charge to require the free-spending Henry III to consult what became the first representative Parliament, creating a system where kings were kept in check by the Lords on whom they relied to enforce their rule. In 1297, the Earls of Norfolk and Hereford led the Lords of England in refusing to fight for King Edward I or grant him money until he agreed to abide by the Magna Carta. Edward I consequently signed the Confirmation of Charters, officially enshrining the document into law and ensuring that the King could not tax the people without their consent.
Throughout the following centuries, the gentry and nobility’s resistance to monarchical tyranny meant that England was generally free from the painful taxation and expropriation without compensation that wracked much of the continent. Its common law justice system flourished, and wars were fought as partnerships between a king and his mostly willing subjects. Self-assertion on the part of the aristocracy came to mean Parliamentary service, in which the landed gentlemen in the Commons and peers in the Lords—the same bodies assembled by Simon de Montfort centuries earlier—could legally lead and restrain both king and commoners, thus curtailing the chance of internal conflict. 
In the early modern period, the Lords turned to fight tyrannical efforts from below, pushed by factions of the gentry in the House of Commons. The Levellers and Diggers in Cromwell’s coalition were stomped out when they attempted to effect social revolution alongside a political revolution against Stuart financial tyranny. When Levelling returned in the form of Chartism two centuries on, it was the aged Duke of Wellington who led the defense of London and stopped the Chartists’ Kennington demonstration from turning into a revolution. Meanwhile, the Lords and Sir Robert Peel worked through reforming legislation that would address real injustices, namely high bread prices imposed by the Corn Laws, which set tariffs on imported grain. Throughout the ages, the aristocracy struck deals and found compromise solutions as they led opposition to the sources of budding tyranny in the British state.
Between the tempering effects of generational wealth, the chivalric norms of the late medieval age, and the self-conscious sophistication of parliamentary government, the savage Norman lords who sacked England under William the Conqueror became the quintessential civil aristocracy of early modern England. Aspiring to more refined ideals, the elite used the leisure afforded to them to cultivate Classical virtue, self-restraint, and a skill for command that would distinguish them as gentlemen.
Land, Legacy, and Duty
As land was long the safest form of income-producing wealth, it was land into which the riches of the ruling class were invested. On this land they built stately homes, houses that could be called castles, constructed with enormous expenditure of labor and capital that acted as monuments to family legacy, longevity, and leadership over a particular place. From Tattershall Castle to Wentworth Woodhouse, these architectural achievements stand as a testament to the fact that from the feudal until the bureaucratic age, the landed elite were the ones with power. As English historian J.A. Froude once said in a speech titled “On the Uses of a Landed Gentry”, attachment over generations to the same estate and community came “from an ambition to leave our names behind us, rooted into the soil to which the national life is attached.” From that deeply planted ambition, the great names of England’s history grew and flourished, while always maintaining a connection to their roots. 
The Percys, one of England’s oldest and most powerful noble houses, fought the border reivers for generations from the security of their ancestral home of Alnwick Castle. Sir Winston Churchill’s ancestor, the Duke of Marlborough, returned from his military triumph in the War of the Spanish Succession to anchor his name on the baroque splendor of Blenheim Palace. Coke of Norfolk used the Neo-Palladian Holkham Hall and estate he inherited for agricultural experimentation that shaped history, contributing to the British Agricultural Revolution that would feed future industry. 
In each case, the estate supported the noble house, and the house supported the dynasty. Through this process, the English aristocracy both strengthened their familial standing and set about imprinting their ideals upon the nation, particularly as the disorder prior to the 1688 Glorious Revolution gave way to a centuries-long domestic peace. As English historian Lawrence James writes in Iron Duke, “all that today we most admire about eighteenth-century Britain, its architecture, music, landscape gardens, literature and scholarship” came thanks to these leading families of gentlemen. Their country homes represented splendour, pride, and a strong belief in the future that proliferated throughout the country. They commanded armies, cultivated culture, and guided the nation, resting their legitimacy on their leadership of the state in numerous endeavors.
The nation was suffused with their ethos of dutiful service and sense of dignity over this century, and it came to dominate Britain as a whole in the Victorian period that followed, with the British middle class being remarkable for the degree to which it accepted the cultural values of the landed elite. This attitude only increased as the 19th century wore on; as historian J.V. Beckett writes in The Aristocracy in England, “one of the most poignant images of late Victorian England was the desire for state honours, in the form of knighthoods and other orders, which suggested a concern with establishment recognition rather than with bourgeois values.” 
That Blenheim Palace rose and Chatsworth House was largely rebuilt during the 18th century was no accident; the homes represented the continuation of family legacy and new investment that domestic tranquility allowed. Enshrined in stone at no small cost, such houses served as testaments to the future and longevity of the families they sheltered. The buildings were expressions of confidence in the future and of the prospects of the family, something that remained true as houses had to be renovated to be equipped with the accoutrements of the future, from plumbing and gas to electricity and the telephone.
To maintain these monuments of family heritage required diligence and dedication. That such estates could be supported for centuries was due to a multi-generational process of upkeep and reinvestment in the property. Renovating an estate to support a palatial house was an expensive process, necessitating enclosure, field drainage, and animal husbandry. These recurring capital-intensive improvements made British estates significantly more productive than the small farms of the continent by allowing for the use of formerly waterlogged fields and cultivation of a higher quality of English livestock. 
Without gentlemen such as Coke of Norfolk funding and promoting such innovations—Coke encouraged the adoption of his improved sheep breeds and demonstrated how drainage and marling had turned even the sandy soil of his Holkham estate arable—it is unlikely that the British Agricultural Revolution would have happened at all, or the Industrial Revolution it fed. For the gentry to invest in such massive and costly innovations required long time horizons and collaboration with tenants rather than exploiting them for additional rent or resources. Capital in the form of land was functionally different from other kinds as it required continuous upkeep and attention from its owner.

Propagating this legacy-conscious mindset across generations was not driven purely by the needs of their particular type of capital. Even today, one of the most reliable ways to secure your own legacy is by having a building in your name; if your family has use of it so much the better. But it is important to emphasize that aristocrats occupied what was in many ways an incredibly restrictive lifeworld, one where families rather than individuals functioned as the basic unit of account, and social status was explicitly tied to one’s lineage. 
Such restriction channeled personal ambition and, through this economic and social discipline, helped forge a functional elite class, a class sometimes willing and capable of shouldering immediate financial burdens for the long-term benefit of the country and its governance. Throughout the 18th century, land taxation fell primarily upon the shoulders of the British landowner elite, something these landowners mostly accepted, seeing it necessary to defeat the French without causing a domestic tax revolt. 
The British landed elite enjoyed remarkable popularity throughout the 19th century, despite owning a significantly higher portion of the land than their continental counterparts. The 1873 Return of Owners of Land survey found that roughly seven thousand families owned eighty percent of Britain, with nobility owning nearly a third of the nation’s land and another half going to the gentry. We can credit the landed elite’s popularity in the face of this enormous inequality to the fact that they viewed land ownership as inextricable from duty to the people. As 19th-century English architect Sir Gilbert Scott put it:
Wealth must always bring its responsibilities, but a landed proprietor is especially in a responsible position. He is the natural head of his parish or district—in which he should be looked up to as the bond of union between the classes. To him the poor man should look up for protection; those in doubt or difficulty for advice; the ill disposed for reproof or punishment; the deserving, of all classes, for consideration and hospitality; and all for honourable and Christian example.
The process of estate improvement sharpened this understanding of duty, as the exercise of local leadership preserved the domestic tranquility that made investments remunerative by limiting disorder and stimulating population growth. Participation in politics was the foundation of the elite’s security, for, by maintaining control of the government, they could ensure it would defend private property and the privileges it afforded them.
This was particularly true at the parliamentary level, as only by running and winning elections could gentlemen keep Levellers and radicals out of the legislature. In fact, as Miller argues in Origins of the American Revolution, the “remarkable conservatism” of English politics came because the landed elite ensured the revolutionary aspects of the Glorious Revolution “stopped with the aristocracy on top, and there, the Whig Lords maintained, it ought to remain.” So long as they kept hold of the Parliamentary supremacy they created, this was the case. Once they lost their touch and new men of Lloyd George and Ramsay MacDonald’s cut occupied Parliament’s seats, former conservative shibboleths, such as the sacrosanct nature of private property and the conception of the landed elite as duty-bound and privileged to govern the nation, faded away.
This political arrangement proved remarkably durable through the massive technological changes of the Industrial Revolution. Despite a decline in the incomes of the landed gentry caused by the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846, which ended high tariffs on imported grain, as late as the 1880s, nearly half the Commons still came from the landed elite. It was only in the early 20th century that the aristocracy’s involvement in national government, and subsequently their ability to resist centralization, began to dwindle dramatically. By 1910, the seats occupied by landed elites in the House of Commons amounted to roughly ten percent, a sharp decline from fifty percent only thirty years prior. 
The incredible longevity of the British feudal and post-feudal aristocracy—stretching from the end of the Dark Ages to the early 20th century—was due to a governing ethos shaped by their landed responsibilities. In turn, the land and her tenants rewarded those with the foresight and willingness to invest that was required for the flourishing of a country estate. In contrast to the frequent assumption that economic success must come at the cost of one’s character, the British landed elite learned that it was only through embodying high gentlemanly ideals that they could effectively manage their estates and social relations. Only after five hundred years of tutelage by the country estate were the British ready to win and administer an empire.
The Elites Who Built an Empire
The development of the British fiscal-military state that ruled a quarter of the world, and the industrial sector that powered the empire, was in large part due to the landed elite. The infrastructure development that powered Britain’s industrial and imperial 19th-century dominance succeeded because they provided the necessary capital for investment in things like canals, railways, and ports. The landed elite also took a direct role in investing in the colonies and their industries. For instance, as British historian Robert Lacey reports in his book Aristocrats, the Grosvenor family deployed its fortune in the mid-20th century to invest in everything from the settlement of cotton farms in Rhodesia and South Africa to the development of Annacis Island, an industrial hub located off the Fraser River of western Canada.
The British aristocracy demonstrated how traditional norms of noblesse oblige could be applied to modern industry. Foremost in such application of tradition were the Earls of Fitzwilliam. Rooted in the north of England for centuries, they chose to mine the coal discovered on their estate themselves rather than lease their land for royalties. As patrician industrialists, they set the standards in mine safety, provided sick pay to workers, pensions to families of worker casualties, and built schools, churches, and homes for their employees. Families were even given small plots of land on which to grow vegetables or raise livestock. When work in the mines was slow, the Fitzwilliams provided alternative work for the men so they would have a steady income. These innovations in workforce relations came primarily over the course of the mid-19th century, before any such attempts to care for the workforce were common, much less mandated. 
Into the mid-20th century, the Fitzwilliams were among the few coal owners beloved by the miners. When the Minister of Fuel and Power, Manny Shinwell, and the post-WWII Labour government expropriated their property in 1946, their miners went out of their way to protest the injustice of the regime’s depredations. Shinwell ignored them, and open-cast mining subsequently destroyed the estate, bringing open work pits within mere meters of Wentworth Woodhouse, the irreplaceable Fitzwilliam manor. The miners were soon laid off, and the mines closed. Everyone, other than the bureaucrats, became worse off because noblesse oblige was punished in the name of the social equality that post-war nationalization was meant to achieve.
The Fitzwilliams showed how the virtues and values of the landed elite remained relevant into modernity, being preferable to both rapacious plutocracy and socialist tyranny. They represented a different path forward, one characterized by traditional responsibility. This was true of the aristocracy generally: the Lords led the way on matters like worker hours and safety, as demonstrated by the Sadler Report of 1832, the Mines Act of 1842, the Ten Hours Act of 1847, and the Chimney Sweepers Regulation Acts throughout the 19th century. Motivated neither by personal greed nor bureaucratic self-importance, the landed elite tried to steer a middle path that merged their class obligations with the industrial economy. 
Sadly, this effort was destroyed by the likes of Manny Shinwell and Margaret Thatcher, whose government chose hostility rather than magnanimity when it came to worker-capital-government relations by violently crushing a major miners’ strike so that tens of thousands could be laid off. The Fitzwilliams had found alternative work for miners in hard times, the pay for which almost always came at a loss, out of their own pockets. They did so because they felt responsible for the workers and their well-being. 
Perhaps surprisingly, the martial tradition of this class remained intact deep into modernity, far longer than most assume. In the early twentieth century, the last generation of the landed military elite suffered a roughly twenty percent death rate during World War I, a higher proportion than any other class, including the poorest. This last cohort of privileged landed military elites led their men through the bloody Flanders Fields and died on the front line.

It was this same class that led the armies which first won the many colonies of the British Empire and then administered them. For example, Arthur Wellesley (later Duke of Wellington) and his brother Richard Wellesley together conquered much of what became the Raj in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, and Lord Cornwallis reformed its judiciary while serving as Governor-General. The landed elite was intimately involved in the development and administration of colonies as well. That the Colonial Office could rule the empire with a few dozen staff was in no small part because it was filled by gentlemen trained from birth in leadership and governance. Their attitudes were exported to the lands they settled. Virginia’s gentry was imbued with the same ideals of noblesse oblige, tradition, and hierarchy as the cavaliers who gave the Old Dominion its distinctive culture.
At the beginning of the Second Boer War in 1899, three young dukes—Marlborough, Westminster, and Norfolk—served under military commander Lord Roberts. The landed elite had to commit itself to martial duty to retain the respect of those whom it was expected to lead. That it could do so while receiving only nominal pay was only possible because of its long-held estates. Those manors that rose in imitation of medieval fortresses were still irreplaceable military infrastructure at the dawn of our modern era, as they housed elites able to fight and willing to die for their country.

In a deeper sense, the willingness to fight is the foundation of any state. The modern state can somewhat forcibly make citizens into soldiers with conscription, as press gangs jumping out of unmarked vans in Moscow or Kyiv to grab passing young men demonstrate. Yet, even in these states, someone somewhere in the military hierarchy has to be willingly fighting and enforcing the requirements to fight on others. Without the steadfast support of a committed officer corps, armies are often inclined to overthrow their own governments rather than fight wars they’re unwilling to fight. As a corollary, the lower down the military hierarchy this will-to-fight can be found, the less tyrannical the military and the state.  
This is also why reliable military officers are a headache for any social or political constitution. Making them landless employees of the state might seemingly solve the problem, but it creates a perpetual lobby and faction for greater spending and, with it, taxation, leading to endemic corruption as seen in modern Egypt. The country house solves this tricky question of political economy quite elegantly: if property holders are the ones willing to fight, they oppose expropriation. Because these British elites of the early 20th century remained willing to fight, we cannot call them a decadent or dysfunctional elite after all, especially contrasted with their marginalized descendants or the alternative elites of today. Duty, land, and low time preference were complementary forces when it came to military matters. The economic, political, and social worlds of such men were deeply intertwined, much more so than any comparable class today.
Unhousing the Estate
The catastrophe of the 20th century ended the old world of aristocratic patronage and military service. After centuries of relative domestic peace, the People’s Budget of 1909 renewed social conflict with vigor, just as the landed element’s presence in the House of Commons was fading. Its crushing taxes forced the aristocracy to sell and depart from its ancestral land, removing the basis of its economic power and site of its elite formation in the name of the common good. 
The Parliament Act of 1911 did yet more to separate the stewards from the stewardship of Britain. Years of social strife interspersed with social fabric-rending wars followed. Inheritance taxes crept inexorably higher, peaking at eighty-five percent during the Harold Wilson years. Income tax rose similarly, reaching a peak of ninety-nine percent under Winston Churchill’s wartime government, and investment income taxes reached a similar height of ninety-eight percent in the 1970s. 
Symbolic of this era’s destruction of the landed elite was the bureaucratic regime’s malicious destruction of the country houses. Even those who could shoulder the endless levies of the early 20th century saw their homes appropriated during the Second World War. Of the homes that survived and were returned to their owners, many were reduced to near ruins.
The War Office took over Compton Verney in 1940, the seat of the Barons Willoughby de Broke for centuries, and former seat of Lord Willoughby de Broke, leader of the resistance to the People’s Budget and Parliament Act. He was forced to sell it for reasons of personal economy after his resistance to the onerous taxation had failed, and the wear and tear of the war years was unkind to it.
As British historian David Cannadine describes in The Decline and Fall of the British Aristocracy, soldiers billeted in the gorgeous Jacobean Blickling Hall gratuitously smashed the windows and forced down the doors of the state rooms, heavily damaging the home. Worst of all was the fate of Eggington Hall; there, “the army left the house with all the taps running, the ceilings collapsed, and the building had to be demolished.” There was no purpose to this, just wanton vandalism driven by spite and envy. It was in this dire period that Shinwell brought the full force of the British state to bear in destroying the Fitzwilliam estate at Wentworth Woodhouse, an attack that even his contemporaries described as blatant class-hatred.
Bureaucracy replaced the newly unhoused landed elite. What characterized the new political system was a tidal wave of taxation and regulation. Emblematic of the short-term, anti-tradition mindset of this new regime was the Starmer ministry’s recent attempt to levy another twenty percent tax on farms, merely to raise revenue equivalent to the annual amount Britain already provides as aid to foreign farmers. That a drop of foreign aid could be foregone to preserve the livelihood of locals was not a consideration.
The result of generations of such onerous taxation has been the destruction of the old English order. Once, localities were governed by those with centuries-old ties to the land and surrounding population, whose station required them to honor the responsibilities which accompanied their authority over the territory. The loss of face that came with losing acres meant that one could not simply up and leave if local conditions changed for the worse. An estate would have to be sold, and all the social and physical capital accumulated over the centuries liquidated in an instant. The partnership Burke identified between the living and coming generations has been severed, and all the good it contained lost in the process. Such territories are now ruled by the busybody bureaucrats made infamous to the British public by the popular Amazon series Clarkson’s Farm, where permitting authorities are shown getting in the way of every aspect of running the titular farm. 
Today, plutocrats regularly abandon the communities their insouciance and poor political instincts have ruined, as shown by the flight of left-leaning Silicon Valley technologists from California. Dollars are fungible, stocks and crypto move with their owners, and houses lived in for but a few years lack the emotional hold of an ancient farm or family estate. That fungibility creates a compliant and even complicit political nonchalance: one can simply move when conditions grow difficult, because the new non-landed elite rarely gets involved in the welfare of their communities.
What we now have are plutocrats with riches disconnected from duty. They easily decamp from one jurisdiction to the next, so strings of disasters follow from their refusal to get involved in politics, even to defend law and order or free enterprise. The Anglo-American gentry of ages past served as Justices of the Peace to maintain order; now those who themselves flee disorder do no such thing. They have neither the incentive nor the sense of responsibility necessary to participate in government, to maintain ties to a specific place and its people, or to train themselves in virtue and the art of good governance. 
Instead, they remain fashionable by spending their lives supporting the side of entropy and disorder. They finance political movements that propagate dysfunction in the name of equity or equality because doing so is popular—a trend Tom Wolfe noted decades ago in Radical Chic and Mau-Mauing the Flak Catchers that guilt and status-seeking lead the rich to embrace those who would destroy them—then abscond when the politicians they supported ruin the place from which they came. Look no further than those who now bemoan and flee the expropriatory taxes the candidates their donations supported are attempting to enact.  
The death of duty has been a social cancer. Would our plutocrats die in the trenches at a mortality rate of one in five, as the Old Etonians bravely did, or might such a shocking proposition coincide with diagnoses of heel spurs or asthma which would regrettably prevent such a sacrifice? Are the residents of the luxury neighborhoods in our cities keen to escape jury duty, or do they aspire to emulate their Justice of the Peace ancestors? Do the affluent, our modern equivalents to the landed gentry, use their privileged positions to speak out publicly on important and controversial matters such as crime? We know the answers to these questions. Our economic elite, and the bureaucracy they delegate to manage the decay, aptly avoid the upper-class obligations that used to define and justify their social station.
Generational Projects Need Generational Wealth 
Death taxes accompanied by a general cultural change expressed in movements such as “Die with Zero” have thoroughly separated wealth from duty and ownership from responsibility. Such efforts have achieved what their creators intended, which was to destroy the landed elite and its virtues while pushing that power into the hands of bureaucrats. This process is not unique to Britain, but pervasive across all Western countries. Assets are no longer seen as the foundation of a dynasty that could carry one’s ideals into future ages, but as a mere lemon from which an immediate return can be squeezed and then tossed aside. The concept of germinating and tending to one’s wealth so that it will one day bear even more fruit is now considered to be either a fool’s errand or the mission of a megalomaniac.
Despite this, some men still try to use their wealth to uphold a greater ambition across generations. Elon Musk’s work to preserve free speech online and extend our access to outer space is an echo from a time when duty was still the North Star of the economic elite. The industrialist’s choice to embark upon a bold and multi-generational project to settle Mars, instead of living hedonistically and disbursing what remains to professional philanthropists, consistently earns him fierce critique instead of praise.
Similarly, the upper-middle class is never encouraged to think of itself as potential new gentry, with children who could serve and better their country for generations. Rather, they are taught to conceive of themselves as transient wealth, based on the premise that they hold fortunes made incidentally and not as a consequence of individual prowess or familial character. Without a legible and legitimate social role to fill in our civilization, they are told, and themselves assume, that their descendants will live much as they did, spending life on a white-collar financial treadmill as the highest possible contribution to society, all the while surrendering accumulated social and financial capital to an already far too powerful ecosystem of non-governmental organizations. Those working in tech are from this same milieu, and while they sometimes post on X about achieving “generational wealth,” they have no clear answer as to what generational wealth is for.
The cost of surrender to such a mindset is everything the Western man once held dear. The reward is freedom from the pressure of living up to the achievements of one’s ancestors. When society has grown so dysfunctional that the purpose of life is reduced to the mere pursuit of fleeting pleasure, it is impossible to conceive of building a dynasty devoted to greatness, and we are absolved of the shame for failing to reach the standards set by those who came before us. 
A civilization only thrives, in the words of Cicero, “when old men plant trees that will benefit only another generation,” and say “I should not merely receive these things from my ancestors, but also hand them down to posterity.” Old men don’t plant such trees in a land which tells them that doing so is selfish and immoral. Even if they have no care for public opinion, such investment in the future is rendered impossible if they can reasonably foresee that the forest they hope to cultivate will be taxed into oblivion anyway.
Civilization is a partnership. This compact was physically represented by the great British dynasties and their country seats, embodying a choice to build the future while honoring the past, not wallowing in frivolous decadence or the mendacious languor of state-enforced equity. To recover a governing elite guided by duty and virtue in the manner of George Washington or Lord Salisbury, we must recover the mindset that maintained the landed elite for a millennium: a recognition that there is more to life than the present moment, and we must enable great men to build great things. 
Becoming a multiplanetary species, creating the prosperous and dynamic future of which our ancestors dreamed, and building a world in which great men can flourish and not be crushed by the heavy yoke of the bureaucratic state: this is the task of a new aristocracy, of a new set of men and women guided by a legacy that persists quietly in the beautiful buildings we all cannot help but revere. It is by necessity a multi-generational compact, a decision to embark upon an infinite game far into the future, guided by timeless precepts found in the pages of Plutarch. We must reject the presentism and false pretense of dynasty-destroying tax policies and noxious philanthropic pressures. Instead, we must embrace the idea that wealth carries with it duties of civic participation on behalf of the long-term interest of the people, that virtue is required of those who seek to lead in such a capacity, and that these responsibilities are best conceived of as a partnership between generations past, present, and future. 

Will Tanner, a graduate of Washington & Lee University and the Wake Forest School of Law, is the author of The American Tribune newsletter. You can follow him at @Will_Tanner_1.
